forces: Piano, flute, oboes, bassoons, horns and strings
performers: Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra, Malcolm Sargent
question: How does a nearly continuous accompaniment support such unsettled harmony?
intro: Repeated triplets and plucked bass notes support a melody that repeatedly leans into dissonance. When the piano takes it up, Mozart changes both the texture and the route through the keys.

sections.label: Orchestral statement
sections.mNote: muted strings introduce the melody and its harmonic tensions

sections.label: Solo expansion
sections.mNote: piano takes the melody beyond its opening shape

sections.label: Central dialogue
sections.mNote: orchestral responses and solo phrases lead through changing keys

sections.label: Distant return
sections.mNote: opening melody returns in A♭ before recovering F

sections.label: Home-key close
sections.mNote: F major regains its place through the final phrases

cues.title: Three layers of motion
cues.text: The opening separates a sustained violin melody, repeated triplets in the inner strings and plucked bass notes. Listen to the accompaniment as two different kinds of movement beneath the tune, not as a single soft background.
cues.evidence: The full score, Broude reprint, p. 31, shows muted violins and violas, repeated triplets and pizzicato cellos and basses. The melody follows the first accompaniment bar. The report places a very quiet start before the rise around 0:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Softness does not remove tension
cues.text: Across the orchestral statement, accented dissonances interrupt the melody’s long line. A note can press against the harmony even within muted, restrained scoring; follow its resolution rather than assuming that a quiet texture is harmonically still.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 31–32 marks accented dissonances and wind support within the opening statement. The report rises around 0:35–0:45. The cue concerns the passage’s written tension, not an identified chord attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep the accompaniment in view
cues.text: Through the opening’s changing harmonies, the repeated accompaniment provides continuity. Listen for the difference between a steady pattern and a settled key: one can remain familiar while the other becomes uncertain.
cues.evidence: The score retains the accompaniment through the orchestral introduction’s major- and minor-coloured phrases. The report’s 0:55–1:15 span changes pitch distribution without a comparable interruption of the sound; no machine chord labels are published.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A concerto for Mozart
cues.text: Mozart is the soloist at the concerto’s first performance in March 1785. The advertisement also promises improvisation on a fortepiano fitted with a pedal keyboard; it does not establish that this Andante uses that attachment.
cues.evidence: The National Arts Centre programme note quotes the March 1785 advertisement and describes the pedal keyboard: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107. The distinction between advertised improvisation and concerto scoring is retained.

cues.title: The pulse changes hands
cues.text: In the solo version, the piano carries both the melody and much of the triplet motion, while plucked strings mark out the harmony. The same accompaniment idea now sits inside the soloist’s two-handed texture.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 32–33, from bar 23, transfers triplets to the piano’s left hand over pizzicato strings. The report’s lower level and brightness around 1:50–2:20 support the solo handover; the 2:06 and 2:20 boundaries do not fix individual notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A melody can depart
cues.text: The piano does not simply repeat the orchestra’s statement. Across the solo span, new phrases and ornamented continuations lead beyond the first melody, while the persistent accompaniment helps the ear connect the changing material.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 33–35 and Hannah Chan-Hartley’s programme account describe the solo expansion. The report has a rise at 2:45 followed by a change of spectral balance around 2:50–3:05; the cue does not assign a theme to one second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Familiar shapes, changed harmony
cues.text: Within the solo expansion, familiar melodic gestures move into a C-centred region rather than staying in F major. Listen for how the same kind of phrase acquires a different tension when its bass and accompanying chords change.
cues.evidence: The score’s middle solo passage moves through C minor and C major; pp. 34–35 show the altered notes and sustained wind harmonies. The report changes from quieter 3:15–3:25 windows to a fuller 3:35–3:50 span, supporting a broad passage description.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A later film association
cues.text: Bo Widerberg’s 1967 film Elvira Madigan uses this Andante and gives the concerto its later nickname. The soundtrack uses Géza Anda’s recording, not Schnabel’s 1937 performance heard here.
cues.evidence: The work’s reception account identifies the film, date and Anda recording, with references to Michael Steinberg and Allen Hughes: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._21_(Mozart)#Cultural_references

cues.title: An orchestral answer
cues.text: In the central dialogue, the orchestra answers the piano with more concentrated gestures before the solo line resumes. The accompaniment’s pulse persists through changes of speaker, linking the exchanges instead of letting each one become a separate song.
cues.evidence: Score p. 35, bars 55–61, alternates tutti and solo. The report rises strongly at 4:30–4:35 and changes at 4:42 and 4:56. The section marker groups this dialogue rather than timing every exchange.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The harmony grows sharper
cues.text: The middle passage intensifies the clashes between the melody and its supporting chords. Listen for the small resolutions inside the larger phrase: Mozart makes the return necessary by allowing the apparently gentle material to become unsettled.
cues.evidence: Score p. 36, bars 62–72, shows the accented dissonances and the lead towards the reprise. Strong changes at 5:26 and 5:30 anchor this broad harmonic turning point; individual chords are not identified from the analysis.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune returns elsewhere
cues.text: The opening melody returns in A♭ major rather than immediately recovering F major. Recognise its shape before waiting for the home key: thematic return and harmonic return are deliberately separated.
cues.evidence: The score’s reprise begins around bar 73, across pp. 36–37; the National Arts Centre note explicitly identifies its A♭-major start. The report’s 5:42–5:46 changes support an approximate 5:48 marker, not a precisely aligned tonic chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A preserved mono performance
cues.text: The digital file is Bob Varney’s transfer from Angel’s mono LP COLH 67. The orchestra’s discography dates that reissue to November 1959, more than twenty years after the Abbey Road session.
cues.evidence: Archive description: https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21. LSO discography session 0158 dates COLH67 to November 1959: https://londonso-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/08/Discography-August-2024.pdf#page=289

cues.title: Finding F again
cues.text: Across the later return, the harmony works back towards F major. Listen beneath the embellished piano line for the recovering bass foundation; the melody has become familiar again before the tonal route is fully resolved.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 37–39 and the National Arts Centre account establish the route back to F. The report changes around 6:24 and reaches a contrasting, quieter span at 7:00–7:05. This marker begins the closing region, not an exact first F-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pattern outlasts the phrase
cues.text: In the closing stretch, the piano’s ornaments and the orchestra’s held notes still move at different rates. Follow the repeated accompaniment through the phrase endings: its persistence makes the final release different from an ordinary breath between melodies.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 38–39 retains the accompaniment beneath late piano figures and sustained wind harmonies. The report shows contrasting spectral balance at 7:25–7:40 and a boundary at 7:42; no isolated ornament is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pulse is released
cues.text: The closing F-major cadence allows the repeated motion to stop. Listen to the difference between the last articulated notes and the resonance that remains after them; the ending releases an accompaniment that has carried almost the whole movement.
cues.evidence: Score p. 39 ends the triplet accompaniment and closes in F major. Relative level falls at 8:10–8:15 and detected attacks disappear in the final window. The exact release is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The piano inherits the inner pulse
transitions.how: The orchestra completes its F-major statement and withdraws. At the solo entry, the piano’s left hand takes over the triplet accompaniment while the strings become pizzicato; the right-hand melody follows above that new texture. Continuity comes from the repeated pulse, but the shift from bowed strings to keyboard changes the way melody and accompaniment are connected.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 32, bars 22–26. The report falls markedly from 1:40 to 1:50–2:00, with boundaries at 1:48 and 1:52. The 1:50 marker estimates the handover, not the first solo note.

transitions.title: The orchestra interrupts the solo continuation
transitions.how: The solo expansion reaches an orchestral response rather than settling into another complete opening statement. Winds and strings condense the phrase, then the piano answers over the continuing bass pulse. The exchanges carry the harmony beyond the C-centred solo span towards the movement’s more unsettled central passage.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 35, bars 55–61, supplies the alternating tutti and solo. Relative level rises at 4:30–4:35; structural changes follow at 4:42 and 4:56. These features anchor the dialogue as a passage.

transitions.title: The melody returns before the home key
transitions.how: Accented dissonances give way to a short easing of the accompaniment and a connecting piano phrase. When the opening melodic shape returns, it is placed in A♭ major, not F major. Restoring the triplet texture and the tune therefore does not complete the tonal return: Mozart leaves the harmony further work to do.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 36–37, bars 68–76, and the National Arts Centre account document the interrupted pulsation and A♭ reprise. Changes at 5:26–5:30 precede further boundaries at 5:42 and 5:46; 5:48 is an approximate reprise marker.

transitions.title: The returned melody recovers its footing
transitions.how: The reprise does not remain in A♭. Altered notes and connecting phrases lead through minor-coloured harmony towards F major again, while piano and winds continue to share the melodic work. The familiar accompaniment survives the modulation, so the recovery of the home key feels like a gradual clarification rather than a separate new section.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 37–39 supplies the tonal route and continuing accompaniment. The report places a broad change after the 6:30–6:55 swell, with quieter 7:00–7:05 windows. The marker denotes a closing region, not a precisely located cadence.

source.title: Mozart, K. 467, full score: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1878; Broude reprint, plate 422
source.locator: II, printed pp. 31–39. Trumpets and timpani are absent. Passage-level snapshots are proportioned to the audio report, not individual entrance timings; the exact performing edition is unestablished.

timeline.note: Opening accompaniment: muted inner-string triplets above pizzicato cellos and basses precede the melody.
Opening melodic passage: muted first violins sing above the two-layer string accompaniment.
Orchestral statement: woodwinds and horns colour the accented harmonies and answer the string line.
Solo statement: piano triplets and melody unfold over pizzicato strings.
Solo expansion: bowed string figures return beneath the piano’s changing phrase shapes.
Central orchestral response: winds and strings take the foreground before another short piano answer.
Central dialogue: solo phrases, sustained wind chords and string accompaniment alternate within the passage.
Distant reprise: piano restores the opening shape over plucked strings, with oboe and bassoon support in the surrounding phrases.
Closing region: piano ornaments, held winds and the repeated string pulse lead back to F major and the final release.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Artur Schnabel (piano), London Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: The item description, source LP sleeve and LSO discography agree. The later sleeve’s title Sir is not used to infer Sargent’s title at the 1937 session.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any local editorial changes are not identified. The consulted full score establishes the movement’s original forces, including the absence of trumpets and timpani, but is not claimed to be the copy used at the session. The Archive description explicitly says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current attribution follows the corrected record. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: LSO session 0158 dates K. 467 to 12 January 1937; the 9 January date in the same entry belongs to K. 459. Both Andante sides are dated 12 January in the side-level discographies.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The item names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
fields.note: The Archive expressly identifies a mono LP transfer. Angel is the transferred reissue label; the original shellac issue was on His Master’s Voice.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: COLH 67 is visible on the photographed sleeve, which pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. The LSO discography dates the LP to November 1959 and the original K. 467 set, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. The Andante occupied DB3101.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4608-1 and 2EA 4609-2A; Andante parts 1–2 on HMV DB3101, concerto sides 5–6.
fields.note: The original issued matrices and takes are documented in both discographies, but their identity within this particular LP transfer has not been established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No side-join timing is assigned. A targeted DAHR search did not yield a usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit source credit is ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; it is not an assumption based on the uploader’s identity.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: 19 April 2010 is the item’s added date, not an identified transfer date. The later current-file timestamp and the correction notice likewise do not establish when the LP was digitised.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No cartridge, equalisation, restoration, editing or speed-correction procedure is documented. Internet Archive describes the file as original-upload VBR MP3; that descriptor does not imply access to an original recording master.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 authorship term.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791. The consulted public-domain full score derives from Breitkopf’s 1878 edition. This term calculation concerns the underlying composition and does not establish rights in an unidentified modern performing edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
fields.note: Publication before 1963 is documented by the orchestra’s discography, not inferred only from the session date. The ordinary EU 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This is a territorial basis, not worldwide clearance. US public-domain status is not established; the recording was not first published by 1925. The uploader’s http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/ declaration does not independently establish authority to clear the original performers’ or producer’s rights in the US or elsewhere. The legal link below identifies the term basis rather than a Creative Commons licence.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
